clue.text: Allies Day

definitions.meaning: first meaning: joins together, as in marriage, a verb
second meaning: the common short form of the third weekday

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it suggests VE Day or a wartime commemoration; the two words are separate meanings. One is a verb (allies itself with), the other the abbreviation for Wednesday.
explanation.definitionFit: To ally two things is to unite or marry them, and the midweek day is commonly abbreviated with this four-letter form.

clue.text: At first, Alexander Pope's drinking large Roman brandy

indicators.note: 'at first' asks for only the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

indicators.note: something that drinks takes another thing inside it

parts.note: the poet Alexander Pope was a Roman Catholic, abbreviated RC
the Latin, i.e. Roman, word for large (feminine), as in Magna Carta

explanation.surface: The poet Alexander Pope is pictured downing a big glass of Italian brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope is the 18th-century poet, not the pontiff, though both lead to RC: the poet was a Roman Catholic. 'Roman' tells you to put 'large' into Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a specific spirit distilled in Gascony in south-west France, so it is an example of the broader category.

clue.text: Within limits in dynamics, element's missing in valves

indicators.note: to sit within something is to be enclosed by it
the limits of a word are its two edges, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the word

indicators.note: something missing has gone, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: a chemical element, the halogen with symbol I
taken as written, then removed from the element

explanation.surface: A music or physics note: some element is absent inside the valves, within the range of dynamics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Valves' is the old electronics sense, not heart or trumpet valves; 'in' does double service in the surface but here is simply two letters to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: Thermionic valves, as British usage calls vacuum tubes, include two-electrode types that pass current one way only.

clue.text: Such as haematite, coarser on original raised walls

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising letters makes them read from bottom to top
the words act as walls around the answer, which is tucked inside them

parts.note: a run of letters spanning the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A geology description: haematite is coarser than some original rock, with raised walls.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in coarSER ON ORIginal reading upwards. The definition is plural because 'such as' introduces an example of a class.
explanation.definitionFit: Haematite is a reddish mineral of iron oxide and one of the chief rocks mined for the metal.

clue.text: A snog, is it, by every other shed? Literally dreadful!

indicators.note: shedding every other letter leaves alternate ones in place

parts.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on of this run

explanation.surface: A sulky teenager asks whether a kiss is the reason every other person has been shed — how dreadful!
explanation.walkthrough: Keep A, N, G, S, T, Y from 'A snog is it by'. 'Literally' tells you to take 'dreadful' at its word: full of dread.
explanation.definitionFit: Angst is a feeling of dread or anxiety, so being full of it is being dread-ful in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Scattered produce raised around arid ground runs short

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising letters makes them read upwards
to go around something is to enclose it
being short of runs means the cricket abbreviation for a run is removed

parts.note: farm produce

indicators.note: ground up means crushed and broken, so the letters are reformed

parts.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A farming scene: crops grown on dry land come up thin and patchy where water runs short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' only works because this is a down entry, so the reversed word reads upwards; 'runs short' is a cricket abbreviation lost, not a shortage of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Something occurring only here and there, irregularly and thinly spread, is synonymous with being dotted about.

clue.text: Low-down exploit: nothing escapes charge

indicators.note: whatever escapes gets away, so those letters are lost

parts.note: the low-down is the inside information
to exploit is to make use of
the zero-shaped letter

explanation.surface: A shady scheme: the con has slipped away and nothing will stick, so no charge can be brought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' is the verb meaning to fill, not a legal accusation, and 'nothing' is the letter shaped like zero.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge something with a quality is to fill or imbue it, as a speech may be filled with emotion.

clue.text: Miss one cutting off the wall

indicators.note: something cutting into another splits it and sits within

parts.note: off the wall means crazy
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A footballer misses the shot as one ball cuts off the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' is a young unmarried woman, not a failure to hit; 'off the wall' is one idiom for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Maid is an old word for a girl or unmarried woman, the same person once addressed by the title used here.

clue.text: Lord Rothermere finally seen in press just this morning?

parts.note: a peer's rank

indicators.note: to be seen in something is to be inside it

parts.note: to press clothes is to iron them

indicators.note: finally points to only the closing letter of the word

parts.note: the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: Viscount Rothermere, the newspaper proprietor, has appeared in the press only today.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' sends you to newspapers because of the press baron Rothermere, but it is the verb meaning to iron. The question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: This morning is an instance of a time before now on the same day, the period the phrase refers to.

clue.text: A bit of nosh fills hole, followed by a bottle of milk

indicators.note: whatever fills something goes inside it

parts.note: a pit is a hole in the ground

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small part of it, here just its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A snack fills a gap in your stomach, washed down with a bottle of milk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of nosh' looks like a snack, but it means one letter. Pinta is British slang from an old advertising slogan, 'Drinka Pinta Milka Day'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinta is informal British for a pint of milk, the standard size of glass bottle once left on doorsteps by milkmen.

clue.text: Rocks, put through the mill and then inserted, remain solid

indicators.note: inserted means placed inside something else

parts.note: rocks are stones
taken as written
milled grain has been ground

explanation.surface: Rocks crushed in a mill and packed back in will hold firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' is not a joining word here: those three letters are the ones inserted into the rocks, with the milled word following.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means refusing to give way or retreat, holding firm under pressure.

clue.text: One's off the drugs now one's run out

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recovering addict says they are clean now that their supply has run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run out' looks like the cause of quitting, but 'run' is fodder and 'out' the signal. The definition takes in 'now', since the person has stopped.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who no longer takes narcotics is a former consumer, described with a hyphenated term for a person who abstains.

clue.text: Women, in a sequence; ladies an inspection may reveal, from top or bottom

definitions.note: plural: women's names, and also hidden messages in a crossword grid

indicators.note: reading from the bottom of a down entry runs letters upwards, against the usual direction
revealing means uncovering something that was concealed in plain sight

parts.note: a run of letters spanning the end of the first word, the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Women stand in a line for inspection, viewed from one end or the other.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords a Nina is a hidden message in the grid, often along the top or bottom row. Here the letters hide in ladieS AN INspection and read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Nina is a girl's name, and crossword slang for a concealed sequence of letters in the grid, so both readings fit.

clue.text: Outings involving such performers could be soul-destroying

indicators.note: could be suggests one set of letters may become another arrangement
the letters involve another word, which must be taken back out to leave what remains

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then removed

explanation.surface: Trips out with a certain kind of singer could be a dispiriting experience.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a composite anagram: OUTINGS plus the answer, rearranged, make SOUL-DESTROYING. Strike OUTINGS from those letters and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names singers who alternate rapidly between chest voice and falsetto, an Alpine tradition, so they are a kind of performer.

clue.text: Old Nick elevating new man for big delivery job

indicators.note: elevating lifts something to a higher place, here into an earlier spot in the downward word

parts.note: Old Nick is a name for the devil
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: The devil promotes a new recruit to a big job delivering goods.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, elevating a letter moves it higher up the column. Swapping Old Nick for Saint Nick is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Christmas is the man who delivers presents to every child in a single night, a job of enormous scale.

clue.text: New Inn infiltrated by CID: notice its unusual subtlety

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters leave their ordinary order
making something new reshapes it, so these letters are rearranged too

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Plain-clothes detectives raid the New Inn pub, and its regulars note how subtly it was done.
explanation.walkthrough: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of a British police force; here its letters are just fodder. 'Nice' is in its old sense of fine or precise.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine, precise difference between things is a subtle point, and nice here keeps its older meaning of exact or delicate.

clue.text: Prayer one's interrupting also breaks for a hymn

indicators.note: to interrupt something is to break into its middle
breaking into a word splits it with something placed inside

parts.note: a prayer is a wish or longing
the Roman numeral for one; the apostrophe-s reads as 'is'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A worshipper's prayer is cut into and broken up to make room for a hymn.
explanation.walkthrough: Two insertions into DESIRE: the I goes in after the D, and the A breaks it again before the last E.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin 'Day of Wrath' is a medieval sequence sung in the Requiem Mass, a sacred song of the Church.

clue.text: Indirectly reference Wagner's nine elevated parts in work

indicators.note: parting something separates it so that another thing sits in the gap

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising letters makes them read upwards

parts.note: NEUN is German for nine, the language of the composer
to work at something is to do it

explanation.surface: Indirect references to Wagner's Ninth, raised to prominence in some musical work.
explanation.walkthrough: Wagner wrote no Ninth Symphony: naming the German composer only tells you to put the number into German.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a verb as well as a noun: to make an oblique or veiled hint about something, rather than mention it directly.

clue.text: For a while, stop during school-time to get it

parts.note: in means during, as in 'in winter'
a school term
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pupil has to stop doing something for a while during term to manage it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the opening phrase, a stop that is only temporary.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a rare verb for suspending or leaving off temporarily, the root of intermittent, so a pause rather than a permanent halt.

clue.text: Sample of retro artistes busking, like guitarists and drummers in bands …

definitions.text: like guitarists and drummers in bands

indicators.note: retro means backward-looking, so the letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: a run spanning the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A taste of retro street performers, the sort of players found in bands.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters hide backwards in artiSTES BUSking. The definition works by example: guitarists and drummers each form a smaller group within a band.
explanation.definitionFit: In set theory, a group wholly contained within a larger group is one of these, as the drummers are within all band members.

clue.text: My apparently trashed hat

indicators.note: apparently invites a literal reading of what follows, so a disposal word becomes placing something inside a receptacle

parts.note: what is trashed is binned, put in the bin
Cor! is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'My!'

explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is the exclamation, not the possessive; put its synonym COR in a BIN, which is what being trashed means.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-cornered cocked hat, as worn by Napoleon and naval officers, is a type of headgear named for its two points.

clue.text: Attend performance of Porridge broadcast from stage

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard rather than read, so go by the sound

explanation.surface: Going to watch the classic prison sitcom Porridge as it goes out on air, adapted from a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: Porridge was a BBC sitcom set in a prison, and 'porridge' is British slang for a prison sentence; the nick is slang for jail.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to theatre scenery, the painted sets and backdrops on a stage, as in scenic design.

clue.text: … top singer doing back catalogue

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters run right to left

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, with the 1 read as I
a tit is a small songbird
something that is on is happening

explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' is a bird in crosswords, here the tit; A1 becomes AI. The definition is a rare word for a register or list.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a rare Latin-derived term for a register or list, especially of church dignitaries, so it means an inventory or roll.

clue.text: Is America unable to promote half of Florence?

indicators.note: promotion moves something up, so the back portion goes to the top of the word

parts.note: turn the question into its answer form, 'Can't US?'

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Is America unable?' as 'Can't US?', giving CANT-US; move the second half to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Florence is the capital of Tuscany, so things belonging to the city belong to that Italian region too.

clue.text: Are sailors behind ship's gathering agreed this device will raise water?

explanation.definitionFit: This is an ancient machine with a helical blade inside a tube; turning it lifts water uphill, so it is a pump for irrigation.

clue.text: Explosives — live — tick!

parts.note: as in 'I am', to exist or live
a tick is a moment, informally a mo

explanation.definitionFit: Ammunition, of which this is the informal short form, covers shells and bombs, so it includes explosive charges.

clue.text: Console guards close to bleak site for collaborative work

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.definitionFit: A website that any of its users can edit, like Wikipedia, is built by many contributors working together.

clue.text: Solo in musical show set on Manhattan's West Side

clue.text: Medium of writer, Fleming for one, with something similar on cycle
